newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-SKIERS SEEK TIGHTER DRUG TESTING.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-SKIERS SEEK TIGHTER DRUG TESTING.

text.p: Skiers and coaches at the world championships are calling for improved dope testing to avoid charges of drug abuse.

While there has been thorough testing at the current championships, the International Ski Federation (FIS) acknowledged controls at World Cup events were sporadic and could not reveal how many skiers had been tested this season.

"I cannot tell you how many races will have controls or how many skiers will be tested," said Dr. Peter Jenoure, secretary of the FIS medical commission, who is overseeing drug testing at the world championships.
Under the current FIS doping policy racers only face compulsory testing at the world championships and Olympics, and then only if they finish on the podium or are among two others selected at random.
The arrangement means some skiers could go their entire careers without being tested.
No Alpine skier has tested positive at a major event since France's Christelle Guignard at the 1989 world championships in Vail. She had taken bronze in the giant slalom.

FIS general secretary Gian Franco Kasper insisted that testing has been carried out at five of the 29 World Cup races so far this season, with further checks possible at two of the remaining seven events.

But coaches from Sweden, France, Canada, United States and Austria told Reuters they could not recall any women being tested and believed the only controls conducted on men were at Chamonix and Wengen.

"On the World Cup we test at five to seven events a year and it is surprise control, we do not announce it," said Kasper. "We also have out of competition controls during the summer where we test approximately 150 to200 athletes.
"We could test every race but I don't think it is necessary.
"We have races all winter long, if you take steroids it is normally for just one major event in a certain period.
The problem is that FIS has no independent drug testing policy, relying instead on its member associations to police the sport.
Other than a simple request, FIS does little to encourage testing. Organisers of races, in fact, must pay for any testing themselves and few appear prepared to do so.
According to FIS policy, it cannot refuse any national doping commissions that arrive at a race unannounced to conduct controls.

But at last year's World Cup finals in Lillehammer, when a team from the Norwegian Olympic doping commission arrived to test skiers they were denied access to the athletes by FIS World Cup race director Kurt Hoch.
"They showed up and demanded to test the skiers but had no papers," said Hoch. "Nobody gets tested unless there is a paper signed by Mr. Kasper and they didn't.
"We can't allow just anyone to come in and say they're testing skiers."
Many skiers maintained they would welcome regular testing on the World Cup circuit.
"Right now I think their (FIS) random testing is pretty selective," said Canada's Cary Mullen, who has himself been the subject of rumoured steroid use and who denies it.
"I've never been tested on the World Cup. I get tested up to six times a year by our own association and at national championships but never on the World Cup.
"I'd welcome some type of regular testing."
For the first time in several years the whispers of drug abuse heard around the circuit surfaced into audible concern.
After the Austrian ski team dominated the early part of season Italy's Kristian Ghedina described some of them as being "all colossal" but did not mention drugs.
Italian newspapers made various insinuations but the Austrians laughed them off as nothing more than a healthy diet of schnitzel.
"I know that even the athletes aren't satisfied with the current state of affairs," said Canadian Ken Read, a former World Cup racer and a member of the IOC's athletes commission.
"I know that three years ago the then top 15 had requested to FIS that it conduct in and out of competition testing in response to all the whispers of drug use that were going on at the time.
"Some countries can be trusted and others, well, we have no idea if they have anything.
"Even the U.S., I don't think have a testing system. They test their athletes before the Olympics and major competitions but all you do there is catch the stupid ones."
